nodes.label: No multi-tenancy
nodes.rationale: S3ClientCredentials carries no bucket allowlist, prefix scope or policy, the active provider is global, and one static backend credential serves every client, so every authenticated client can do everything any other can. If tenant separation is required, run one proxy per tenant with its own KEK, client credentials and backend credential.

nodes.label: What an attacker who takes the proxy gets
nodes.norm_label: what an attacker who takes the proxy gets
nodes.rationale: Everything: the KEK in memory and therefore every DEK ever written under it retroactively, the DEK cache, every plaintext in flight, the backend credential, and every client credential (stored as plaintext, not hashes). There is no key isolation, no HSM path and no signing identity that survives; the proxy is the trust anchor and has to be protected like one.

nodes.label: Breaking Change Guard
nodes.rationale: Version 4.0.0 was cut by accident on 2026-09-07: a coverage pull request was merged with a merge commit, two of its commits carried honest breaking markers and the release automation computed a major nobody had planned. A published tag cannot be withdrawn, so a breaking marker reaching main must be declared in advance rather than discovered afterwards.

nodes.label: Pull-request title and body inspection
nodes.rationale: Under a squash merge the title and body become the commit message the release analyser reads, so they carry breaking markers as much as the commits do. They are attacker-controlled text and are passed through the environment, never interpolated into the script, so shell metacharacters in a title cannot run on the runner. The merge base rather than the recorded base SHA is used so a pull request is not blamed for breaking commits it inherited.

nodes.label: npm clean-install --ignore-scripts under a write token
nodes.norm_label: npm clean-install --ignore-scripts under a write token
nodes.rationale: The job runs before review with a token that can push contents, so a dependency install script does not get to run with it; npm audit signatures then checks provenance attestations and registry signatures of what was installed.

nodes.label: Version Dry Run job
nodes.rationale: ADR 0018 D6: on every pull request into main the release tool computes the next version and prints it, so a major is merged against a number the tool produced rather than a human reading of the commits. Nothing is tagged, changed or released. Same-repository pull requests only, because semantic-release verifies push access with a git push --dry-run before analysing anything and a fork token is read-only.

nodes.label: s3_security block in the shipped examples
nodes.norm_label: s3_security block in the shipped examples
nodes.rationale: The examples still set strict_signature_validation, enable_rate_limiting, max_requests_per_minute, enable_security_logging, max_failed_attempts and unblock_ip_seconds with reassuring comments ('recommended: true', 'Conservative limit'), which is why the README documents them at all: only max_clock_skew_seconds reaches code, and only for pre-signed URLs.

nodes.label: Helm deployment and the missing private-key value
nodes.norm_label: helm deployment and the missing private-key value
nodes.rationale: The chart renders the whole proxy configuration from one `config` value straight into a ConfigMap, so an RSA private key written there is clear text readable by anyone with get configmaps. The key belongs in a Secret referenced as ${RSA_PRIVATE_KEY} and injected through the chart's env list with a secretKeyRef.

nodes.label: No rate limiting
nodes.rationale: enable_rate_limiting and max_requests_per_minute are parsed and validated and then read by no code path; an unauthenticated caller is limited only by what sits in front of the proxy. Shipping no rate limiting is a decision (ADR 0014) and removing the misleading keys is ADR 0013.

nodes.label: H-7 Dead security configuration knobs
nodes.rationale: Six s3_security keys and s3_backend.use_tls are parsed, validated, defaulted and documented and then read by nothing, so no protection exists where the configuration says it does; the failed-attempt map is keyed by an attacker-chosen X-Forwarded-For value and never expires, growing memory without bound. Per-IP limiting is also the wrong tool: a legitimate client is one identity issuing thousands of requests from one address. The decision is to delete the knobs and the map and require any real limiter to arrive with a test that proves it throttles.

nodes.label: The Helm chart does not roll pods on a config change
nodes.norm_label: the helm chart does not roll pods on a config change
nodes.rationale: No checksum/config annotation is rendered, so helm upgrade with a changed config updates the ConfigMap, reports success and leaves the old pods running the old provider alias, key material and integrity mode. An operator told a rotation succeeded while the old key still encrypts every new object has been handed a false statement by the tooling: rule 2 exactly. A kubectl rollout restart after every config change is mandatory until it is fixed.

nodes.label: ListParts still pretends
nodes.rationale: It answers 200 with a fabricated always-empty ListPartsResult and never asks the backend, so a client cannot discover what a multipart upload holds. The fix is ADR 0011: answer it from the proxy's own part table.

nodes.label: Trust boundary between proxy and backend
nodes.norm_label: trust boundary between proxy and backend
nodes.rationale: One boundary matters: above it everything is operator-controlled and handles plaintext, below it everything is adversarial. A second, weaker boundary between client and proxy is defended by SigV4.

nodes.label: No backward compatibility
nodes.rationale: Unnecessary code is removed rather than kept compatible; the legacy config migration and the unprefixed metadata fallback are named deletion candidates. This is what lets the stored-object format change without a migration path.

nodes.label: Operations refused with 501 or 422
nodes.rationale: Unrouted sub-resources used to fall through to the base operation for their HTTP method, which is how DELETE /bucket?encryption deleted the bucket; only allowlisted query parameters reach a base operation now. Four object sub-resources answered 200 for work done wrongly or not at all (legal-hold always set the hold ON) and now refuse. CopyObject and UploadPartCopy answer 422 NotSupportedWithEncryption because a server-side copy runs inside the backend where the proxy cannot re-encrypt.

nodes.label: The S3 backend is hostile
nodes.rationale: The backend is assumed able to read, change, swap, roll back, truncate and lie in listings, metadata, ETags and errors. Nothing the backend says or does counts as authentication: '200' and 'the transport was TLS' are statements about availability and the network, not about the integrity of a stored object.

nodes.label: Handlers refuse rather than pretend
nodes.rationale: Under rule 2, an operation answering 200 for work it did not do is worse than one that refuses. Legal-hold always set the hold ON so a release request applied one; ?attributes returned object bytes where an XML document was expected; UploadPartCopy was unreachable and stored a 0-byte part. All now refuse explicitly.

nodes.label: The three rules
nodes.rationale: 1. Integrity means the proxy verifies; verification by the backend or implied by TLS to it is not integrity when the backend is the adversary. 2. A control that exists only in configuration or documentation is worse than no control, because it gets relied upon. 3. The stored-object format may change without a migration path, on the unconfirmed assumption that no deployment holds data that must stay readable across the change.

nodes.label: Pre-signed URL support
nodes.rationale: Query-string SigV4 is validated alongside the Authorization header form; X-Amz-Expires is mandatory and capped at the AWS maximum of 7 days, and the signing time is bounded by max_clock_skew_seconds, so a URL cannot extend its own lifetime.

nodes.label: Clock skew comes from two different places
nodes.norm_label: clock skew comes from two different places
nodes.rationale: The header form uses a compile-time constant of 900 seconds and ignores s3_security.max_clock_skew_seconds entirely; only the pre-signed form reads the configured value. The documented knob configures half of what its name suggests.

nodes.label: H-2 Per-chunk signatures are never verified
nodes.norm_label: h-2 per-chunk signatures are never verified
nodes.rationale: Accepted: chunk signatures protect the client leg while the adversary is on the backend leg, the seed signature never covered the body, UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD is already accepted, and the SDK chooses unsigned-trailer framing over TLS precisely because transport integrity comes from TLS. Verifying the chain costs real CPU; client checksum verification (ADR 0012) buys most of the benefit for less. Residual exposure: a client signing chunks over plain HTTP.

nodes.label: SigV4 validation, header and pre-signed forms
nodes.norm_label: sigv4 validation, header and pre-signed forms
nodes.rationale: Both forms are required by real clients: Velero signs headers on its data path and uses pre-signed URLs for downloads. Failures return a fixed message per error code, because reflecting the raw error echoed attacker-controlled text and broke the XML on keys containing & or <.

nodes.label: The payload is not authenticated
nodes.rationale: A missing X-Amz-Content-Sha256 becomes UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD rather than a rejection and the pre-signed form defaults to it, so the signature covers the request line and headers, not the bytes. There is also no nonce store, so a captured signed request can be replayed inside the 15-minute window, and /health, /version and the whole monitoring listener are unauthenticated.

nodes.label: TLS listener example (config/aes-tls-example.yaml)
nodes.rationale: Exists because the integration suite needs an HTTPS endpoint: aws-sdk-go-v2 only switches to STREAMING-UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD-TRAILER framing and checksum trailers over TLS, and over plain HTTP that decoder is unreachable, which is how BUG-001 shipped unnoticed.

nodes.label: Performance tests run in isolation
nodes.rationale: The proxy-vs-MinIO comparison contends with the rest of the suite for the same MinIO when they run together, which is what made the 100MB case fail inside the full run and pass on its own.

nodes.label: TLS integration run (checksum-trailer framing)
nodes.rationale: aws-sdk-go-v2 only switches to STREAMING-UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD-TRAILER framing with checksum trailers over HTTPS, so the plain-HTTP run cannot reach that decoder at all. BUG-001 survived a full integration run for exactly that reason; both transports are therefore exercised.

nodes.label: Client checksums are dropped, never forwarded
nodes.norm_label: client checksums are dropped, never forwarded
nodes.rationale: Content-MD5 and x-amz-checksum-* describe the plaintext while the uploaded body is ciphertext, so a digest-checking backend would answer BadDigest for a good upload; responses carry no backend checksum for the mirror-image reason. They are not verified by the proxy either, which discards the integrity intent of clients like kopia that send Content-MD5 on every blob. ADR 0012 closes that.

nodes.label: The License Expiry Is Discovered by a Build, Not by an Environment
nodes.norm_label: the license expiry is discovered by a build, not by an environment
nodes.rationale: D7-D10: one token everywhere (local development copy and CI secret identical), and a check that decodes the exp claim of whichever token the job holds and fails — never warns — when it expires within 14 days, running first in every consuming job and on a daily schedule. It reads the payload without verifying the signature; the binary remains the verifier. Blocking a release on a license clock is deliberate: reissuing takes minutes, and the alternative is the pipeline going red on the day with a message naming the wrong cause. A warning annotation was rejected because the proxy's own 30-day startup warning already existed and was ignored.

nodes.label: The License Is a Fatal Startup Gate
nodes.norm_label: the license is a fatal startup gate
nodes.rationale: D1-D5: license validation is part of configuration validation, fatal, with no degraded or grace-period mode, for every provider type except none. The trust anchor is the RSA public key compiled into the binary and is the only one — a test seam was rejected because it would stop being the only possible anchor. A token without an exp claim is invalid and the generator cannot mint one, because a perpetual license is a commercial decision that must be an explicit claim: previously such a token started the proxy and the hourly runtime check killed it 60 minutes later, blaming an expiry that did not exist. Shutdown never depends on the license, closing a path where every unlicensed shutdown hung forever.

nodes.label: Breaking Changes Collect on One Long-Lived Branch
nodes.norm_label: breaking changes collect on one long-lived branch
nodes.rationale: D7/D8/D11: each unit of work is its own squash-merged pull request into the bundle branch so a single unit can be reverted alone, breaking markers are used freely there because nothing releases from it, and the branch is rebased onto main whenever main moves with the end-to-end suite as the gate. main keeps shipping patches and minors meanwhile. Added 2026-09-09: the previous line receives no releases of any kind once the major is out — 4.0.x and earlier are end-of-life at 5.0.0, because there is one supported line and the old format is one the product no longer describes as fit for an untrusted backend.

nodes.label: Release Dry Run Compared Against the Label
nodes.norm_label: release dry run compared against the label
nodes.rationale: D6, amended 2026-09-09: a dry run of the release tool on every pull request into main prints the computed next version and fails when the computed bump and the label disagree in either direction; it writes no tag, changelog or release, and the final merge of a major is made against that printed number because a tag cannot be taken back. Known exposure: the dry-run job holds a token that can push, because the release tool verifies push access before analysing anything — accepted, since the release step runs the same packages with a broader token one step later.

nodes.label: A Major Release Is Declared by the release:major Label
nodes.norm_label: a major release is declared by the release:major label
nodes.rationale: D1-D5: main is the only release branch and the version is computed from Conventional Commits; a pull-request check fails on any breaking marker without the release:major label, reading the added commits, the PR title and the PR body because a merge commit and a squash hand the analyser different text, with deliberately wider marker patterns than the analyser's own since over-reporting costs a label and under-reporting costs a major. Merge commits stay allowed: squash-only was rejected on measured evidence — one truncated changelog line per PR against sixteen lines naming each change, and per-commit notes and per-commit analysis are the same mechanism. Forced by the unplanned 4.0.0 of 2026-09-07, which spent the number reserved for the breaking bundle.

nodes.label: A Rewrite Is Preceded by the Complete Instrument Set
nodes.norm_label: a rewrite is preceded by the complete instrument set
nodes.rationale: D17, added 2026-09-09: ratio thresholds on both listener transports, the ranged-read benchmark with its direct leg, the small-object request-rate benchmark, the key-unwrap microbenchmark, the memory test's numbers and the CPU profiles are all run on the pre-change commit and recorded before the rewrite lands, because a benchmark born after the change has no 'before'. Waiting for the format change and picking thresholds once was rejected: threshold picking is three ordinary runs, while not enforcing means the biggest crypto-path rewrite merges with no gate, and the pre-change table is exactly the 'before' column that rewrite needs.

nodes.label: The CI Gate Is a Proxy-to-Direct Ratio, Never an Absolute Number
nodes.norm_label: the ci gate is a proxy-to-direct ratio, never an absolute number
nodes.rationale: D6-D13, D16: both legs are measured in the same isolated run with the leg order alternating, and the assertion is on the median of at least three per-repetition ratios so one load spike is discarded. Thresholds are recorded from at least three disarmed runs on the actual runner and derived as 20% headroom below the worst observed, re-recorded whenever throughput is expected to move. No switch disarms the assertions, the run cleans every bucket it writes, and absolute throughput is published alongside but never labelled 'the cost of encryption'. Absolute thresholds measure the runner: a 100 MB case failed at 17.6% inside the full suite and passed run alone, which is why the thresholds were disarmed and stayed disarmed.

nodes.label: A Control That Exists Only in Configuration Is Worse Than No Control
nodes.norm_label: a control that exists only in configuration is worse than no control
nodes.rationale: D6, the product's second rule: an announced but unperformed control is worse than an absent one because it gets relied upon. Applied to configuration in ADR 0013 and to the request surface in ADR 0007.

nodes.label: An End-to-End Suite Proves One Client, Never the Scope
nodes.norm_label: an end-to-end suite proves one client, never the scope
nodes.rationale: D5-D7: a change exercised only by the Velero end-to-end suite is not thereby shown safe for anyone else; behaviour every client sees is proven by the integration suites over both transports. Support is claimed only as far as it is exercised, naming which kind of proof it rests on. Defining scope as the set of clients with an e2e suite was rejected because a suite costs a cluster and tens of minutes, so that set would never grow past one or two.

nodes.label: The Integration and E2E Suites Are Part of the Product
nodes.norm_label: the integration and e2e suites are part of the product
nodes.rationale: D1-D4, D9, D14: neither suite is disabled, skipped, weakened or deleted to make a change pass; no switch, flag or configuration value disarms an assertion, and the only legitimate skip is a suite skipping itself when its backend or proxy is unreachable. Work is not finished until both are green, the end-to-end suite gates the release, and a unit test never substitutes for an integration test. Unit tests here assert on a captured request struct against a mock and structurally cannot show that stored bytes decrypt, that a real SDK accepts a composed response, or that a backup tool can restore what it backed up.

nodes.label: Published Key Material Is Rotated, Not Deleted
nodes.norm_label: published key material is rotated, not deleted
nodes.rationale: D7: any deployment that ever ran under a key that appeared in this repository treats every object written under it as compromised — configure a new key, re-write the data through the proxy, then remove the old provider. Removing a literal at the tip does not retract it; the history keeps every key the repository ever contained. D5/D6 close the second routes: the token reaches every environment through S3EP_LICENSE_TOKEN with the local file excluded from the container build context, and the license signing key lives outside the repository, outside any directory a build clean removes, and never in a repository secret — a secret that can mint licenses the shipped binary accepts is a distribution channel, not a backup.

nodes.label: One 256-bit Data Key per Object
nodes.rationale: D1/D2: a fresh random data key per object, never reused, never derived from object key, bucket name or client input; the key encryption key wraps data keys and nothing else and never leaves the process. Deriving the per-object key from master key plus object name was rejected because it records no key identity and makes re-upload reuse the same key, which a nonce-based format must avoid.

nodes.label: Bounded Ranged Read Over Segments
nodes.rationale: D9: a ranged read fetches only the segments the range covers in one contiguous backend request, at most one segment of over-read at each end plus the trailer when the range reaches the end — bounded at 2*65536 + 2*28 + 40 bytes above the returned bytes. No range costs a second backend request and none is served unverified; the accepted cost is 128x amplification on a 512-byte read, with no segment cache added to soften it.

nodes.label: Authenticated Segment Chain (s3ep-gcm-seg-v2)
nodes.rationale: D1-D3: an object is a chain of 65536-byte plaintext segments each sealed with AES-256-GCM under the per-object data key, each carrying its own random 96-bit inline nonce, followed by an authenticated trailer; the format id s3ep-gcm-seg-v2 is written to s3ep-dek-algorithm. Segment size is a constant of the format, not configuration, because making it configurable would make the nonce bound and the stored layout depend on configuration. Derived per-segment nonces (Tink AES-GCM-HKDF) were rejected because S3 multipart is not a single sequential writer and a re-uploaded part would reuse a nonce with different plaintext. Keeping AES-CTR plus per-segment HMAC was rejected as two primitives, two passes and no code deleted.

nodes.label: One Local Key Provider (type aes)
nodes.rationale: D1/D2: exactly one local key-encryption provider, type aes with encryption.providers[].config.aes_key; the rsa type is removed and a configuration naming it does not load. RSA lost on merit: both key halves live in the same configuration so the encrypt-only property does not exist, it unwraps roughly 2400x slower (a benchmark run but never committed), RSA-2048 sits at a 112-bit level against a backend archiving ciphertext forever, and no shipped chart, compose file or e2e configuration uses it.

nodes.label: HashiCorp Vault Transit as the First KMS Backend
nodes.norm_label: hashicorp vault transit as the first kms backend
nodes.rationale: D4/D13: Vault Transit first, AWS and GCP KMS behind the same shape and no earlier; it ships in its own additive release after the 5.0.0 storage format rewrite, because the read path's duplicate data-key unwrap would become a second network round trip per read. The stub that claimed a KMS was never reachable and would have minted a fresh random key per construction, making every restart destroy data — its removal is the first step of the work so no intermediate state looks like a working provider. Deleting the stub outright was rejected because it also deletes the only route to key custody outside the process.

nodes.label: Uniform Segment-Aligned Parts Checked at Complete
nodes.norm_label: uniform segment-aligned parts checked at complete
nodes.rationale: D1-D3, D6: one client part becomes exactly one backend part, a retry replaces its own part and nothing else (fresh segment nonces make repetition safe), and at Complete the proxy checks against its own part table that every part but the highest has the same plaintext size, a multiple of the segment size, encrypted at the offset its number implies, contiguous from 1 — a violation is InvalidPart and aborts. Constraining at write time beats storing a layout, because state that describes the object is state the hostile backend can change or drop. The failure it replaces: an ordered pipeline that blocked a retried or out-of-order part until session expiry, hiding a keystream reuse.

nodes.label: Encryption at Rest Is Asserted by Reading the Backend Directly
nodes.norm_label: encryption at rest is asserted by reading the backend directly
nodes.rationale: D6: never by round-tripping through the proxy, because a proxy that decrypts its own output proves nothing about what was stored. Related evidence rules: every test is shown to fail without the change it covers (D11), an assertion over fetched output is proven at least once to have read something (D12) — several specified checks had never been built and the suite ran past two data-loss defects — and coverage is a floor whose denominator changes are labelled as denominator corrections, after test doubles leaving the production build raised one package from 13.1% to 81.0% with nothing tested.

nodes.label: Hostile Backend Threat Model
nodes.rationale: The S3 endpoint belongs to somebody else, so it is treated as an adversary that can read, alter, swap, reorder, truncate, delete, roll back and lie in listings, metadata, ETags and errors. Adopted because four shipped defects each let 'the backend returned 200 over TLS' stand in for an integrity check: an unverifiable ranged read, a missing-metadata object served as plaintext, integrity that was separable and configurable, and configuration naming protections that did not exist. Rejected: untrusted-but-not-adversarial with TLS carrying integrity, because it fails precisely in the case the product is bought for.

nodes.label: Integrity Is Not Separable From Decryption
nodes.norm_label: integrity is not separable from decryption
nodes.rationale: D4: no configuration key selects, downgrades or disables verification, and no mode yields data plus a log line. Justified by the shipped product: three tolerant modes existed, strict refused nothing on the main path, and every shipped example recommended a mode the code default did not use.

nodes.label: Every Served Byte Is Proxy-Verified at Read Granularity
nodes.norm_label: every served byte is proxy-verified at read granularity
nodes.rationale: D3: a ranged read is verified against the units it overlaps, a whole-object read over the whole object including its length; verification precedes the first byte where the response has not begun, and aborts the body mid-stream where it has. Refusing ranged reads was rejected because it breaks every range-reading client; serving every range by full decryption was rejected as pathological (a 32-byte read of a 20 MiB blob).

nodes.label: A Listing Issues No Per-Object Request, Ever
nodes.norm_label: a listing issues no per-object request, ever
nodes.rationale: D2, named explicitly so it is not proposed again: fetching per-object metadata would turn one backend request into one per key on the hottest read path — a thousand extra requests for a thousand-key page — to fix a byte count. Storing the plaintext size in metadata does not work either (a listing returns no user metadata) and would be a number the backend can edit. This is why the size half is sequenced behind the segment chain, under which the correction is one division per entry.

nodes.label: An Error Behind a Non-Error Status Becomes 500
nodes.norm_label: an error behind a non-error status becomes 500
nodes.rationale: D8: any sub-400 status carrying an error code is answered 500 with the code and message preserved, with 304 Not Modified as the single carve-out because the proxy forwards conditional headers. Real S3 answers some operations 200 with an error document, so this deviates from S3 deliberately: a client that branches on the status code alone must never read a failed operation as success. The carve-out is load-bearing and easy to lose — without it every cache revalidation becomes a 500.

nodes.label: The Multipart <Location> Names the Proxy, Not the Backend
nodes.norm_label: the multipart <location> names the proxy, not the backend
nodes.rationale: D4/D5: the first value of X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-Host when present, otherwise the connection scheme and Host header. No trusted-proxy list guards them because the value is reflected only to the sender and drives no decision inside the proxy, so a forger misleads only itself — which becomes void the moment anything treats the value as trustworthy. A configured public URL was rejected as a configuration key in a release whose direction is deleting keys nothing reads.

nodes.label: The Backend Account Never Appears in a Response
nodes.norm_label: the backend account never appears in a response
nodes.rationale: D10: where an owner element is emitted it names the requesting client's own access key id as both identifier and display name. Costs the truthful answer — a client that genuinely wants the backend account cannot learn it — and the substitute identity is a recorded default, not validated against a strict client.

nodes.label: The Metadata Prefix Is the Proxy's Exclusive Namespace
nodes.norm_label: the metadata prefix is the proxy's exclusive namespace
nodes.rationale: D1/D4/D5/D7: every key the proxy writes carries encryption.metadata_key_prefix (default s3ep-), no key outside its own set may carry it, no code substitutes a literal prefix, every comparison lower-cases first because S3 lower-cases user metadata keys in transit, and every key inside the namespace is stripped from GET, HEAD and ranged responses so the wrapped data key never reaches a client. S3 user metadata is one flat map per object; the prefix is the only thing separating client keys from proxy keys.

nodes.label: Prefix Shape Rule ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{2,}-$
nodes.rationale: D2/D3, amended 2026-09-09: validated at startup, never normalised, lower-cased, trimmed or replaced by the default. The trailing dash puts the namespace end on a word boundary so a prefix cannot capture a client key that merely begins with the same letters; the four-character minimum rules out namespaces like 's3-'. An empty prefix turned the proxy into a shredder (ciphertext served as plaintext behind 200) and honouring it literally is arithmetically wrong, since an empty prefix matches every key — neither branch is correct, which is what makes it a configuration error.

nodes.label: Listings Are Real S3 Documents Built by the Proxy
nodes.norm_label: listings are real s3 documents built by the proxy
nodes.rationale: D4-D6, D9-D11: ListBucketResult / ListAllMyBucketsResult with the S3 namespace, S3 element names and order, millisecond LastModified, absent values as absent elements; no checksum element at all because backend checksums describe ciphertext and the proxy's own is sealed inside the object; Owner is the requesting client's access key id; the proxy always requests URL encoding from the backend and re-encodes only when the client asked. Patching the existing document was rejected — the missing namespace, the SDK-structure elements and the accidental order are one defect, not several.

nodes.label: No Client Checksum Reaches the Backend, No Plaintext Checksum in Metadata
nodes.norm_label: no client checksum reaches the backend, no plaintext checksum in metadata
nodes.rationale: D8/D9: no client checksum value, and no algorithm choice derived from one having been sent, is passed on — asking the backend to check a digest of a plaintext it never receives is incoherent. No plaintext checksum is ever written to object metadata, because a cleartext checksum next to the ciphertext is a confirmation oracle: for a small or low-entropy object the backend can guess a candidate plaintext offline and confirm it.

nodes.label: An Unworkable Configuration Refuses to Start
nodes.norm_label: an unworkable configuration refuses to start
nodes.rationale: D4/D5/D7: the backend transport is the scheme of s3_backend.target_endpoint (a scheme-less endpoint is a startup error), and a plain http:// backend under an encrypting provider refuses to start because the SDK only accepts UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD over TLS and the proxy hands it an unseekable ciphertext reader, so every streaming upload fails with 'failed to seek body to start'. Also refused: an invalid metadata prefix, an out-of-range streaming_segment_size, a non-loopback pprof address while profiling is on, a client secret under 16 characters. No silent normalisation — a value that would have turned the proxy into a shredder fails loudly. Warning instead of refusing was rejected: the process would be healthy and every streaming upload would fail.

nodes.label: Filename Encryption Encrypts Directory Segments Only
nodes.norm_label: filename encryption encrypts directory segments only
nodes.rationale: D1-D3, D9: opt-in under encryption.filename_encryption, off by default; the key is split on '/', every directory segment is encrypted and the leaf is stored in the clear, deterministically and statelessly with no mapping index anywhere the backend can reach. The owner's constraint is that lookups stay exact and reliable, which kills the obvious schemes: encrypting the whole key destroys the partial-leaf prefix listing content-addressed backup clients depend on, a mapping object hands the hostile backend a denial of service and a rollback oracle in one object, and randomised encryption makes an exact lookup impossible. A prefix ending inside a directory segment cannot be translated and returns an empty listing, documented rather than papered over.

nodes.label: An Object Is Readable From Itself
nodes.norm_label: an object is readable from itself
nodes.rationale: D3: the wrapped data key travels in the object's own metadata as s3ep-encrypted-dek; reading needs the object, its metadata and the configured key encryption key, nothing else. A key database or sidecar index was rejected because a bucket restored elsewhere would arrive without it and its loss makes readable ciphertext undecryptable.

nodes.label: Every Response Is Composed by the Proxy
nodes.norm_label: every response is composed by the proxy
nodes.rationale: D1-D3, D6, D7, D11: status, error code, headers and body are values the proxy can state truthfully; bodies are marshalled from typed structures so escaping is a property of the encoder, documents carry S3 element names, root and namespace and only vouched-for elements, backend failures are translated from the typed error rather than by pattern-matching message text, and every failure is an S3 <Error> document. Faithful proxying was rejected under the threat model: a 200 carrying an error document is precisely the answer a hostile backend would choose.

nodes.label: Content-Keyed DEK Cache
nodes.rationale: D9: the cache key includes a digest of the wrapped data key, so a re-upload of the same object key cannot return the previous data key — correctness by construction rather than by write-path invalidation. Fixes a shipped defect where a cache keyed on (fingerprint, object key) served a stale key after a re-upload, producing garbage plaintext and an aborted download. Invalidating from the write paths was rejected because a path missed today or added tomorrow reintroduces the defect silently.

nodes.label: Key Rotation Is a Configuration Procedure
nodes.norm_label: key rotation is a configuration procedure
nodes.rationale: D6/D7/D8: several providers may be configured, encryption.encryption_method_alias names the write provider, all are available for reads. Rotation is add-provider, repoint-alias, restart; there is no re-encryption job and re-writing through the proxy is the migration. Removing a provider makes its objects permanently unreadable, and the restart is part of the rule because tooling that only rewrites configuration leaves the old key encrypting new objects while reporting success.

nodes.label: Associated Data Binds Format Id, Client Object Key and Index
nodes.norm_label: associated data binds format id, client object key and index
nodes.rationale: D4/D5: every seal binds the format id, the client-visible object key and an 8-byte big-endian index (all-ones for the trailer). The bucket is deliberately excluded so a ciphertext bucket can be replicated, copied or renamed without re-encryption — at the accepted cost that two buckets under the same key encryption key can be swapped key-for-key. A configured per-deployment label was rejected as one more stored-format dependency where a mislabel makes a whole bucket unreadable.

nodes.label: A KMS-Backed KEK Is Its Own Provider Type
nodes.norm_label: a kms-backed kek is its own provider type
nodes.rationale: D1/D3/D6: chosen per provider alias, not a mode or flag; the key never enters the proxy, wrap and unwrap are remote, there is no local copy and no path that serves a request while the KMS is unreachable. Runtime failure is fail-closed per request with no fallback, because a fallback is a path on which data is readable without the KMS. A flag on the local provider was rejected: the two differ in fingerprint derivation, failure behaviour, latency and availability — four contracts behind one name.

nodes.label: Server-Side Copy Refused With 422 NotSupportedWithEncryption
nodes.rationale: D9/D10: a PUT carrying x-amz-copy-source and UploadPartCopy are refused, unconditionally — including under the none provider (settled 2026-09-09), because none is not a production mode and one behaviour on the API surface beats a provider-dependent branch. Server-side copy runs inside the backend where the proxy has no plaintext, and under the name binding of the segment chain a backend copy to a different key produces an object undecryptable under its new name — a corruption the client finds at read time. The only future route is a proxy-side fetch-decrypt-re-encrypt, an additive feature for a later release.

nodes.label: Profiling on Its Own Loopback Listener
nodes.norm_label: profiling on its own loopback listener
nodes.rationale: D8: monitoring.pprof_bind_address, default 127.0.0.1:6060, never registered on the metrics listener; only a loopback IP literal or the literal 'localhost' is accepted, because resolving a name at startup makes the proxy unbootable without a resolver and a name pointing at loopback today can point elsewhere tomorrow. The defect: profiling handlers sat on the unauthenticated metrics listener that binds every interface, and a heap profile of this process contains data encryption keys, unwrapped key material and plaintext buffers — anyone reaching the metrics port could recover plaintext without touching the backend, with only a log warning telling the operator to restrict access.

nodes.label: Response Wrappers Preserve Flush, Hijack and ReaderFrom
nodes.norm_label: response wrappers preserve flush, hijack and readerfrom
nodes.rationale: D9: a layer wrapping the response preserves the capabilities beneath it — flushing a partial response, taking over the connection, reaching the underlying writer. A wrapper that silently removes one changes how a long transfer behaves and disables the very mechanism a per-transfer deadline would need. Found the hard way: an observability wrapper removed the fast copy path and the streaming capabilities together, invisibly, because everything still worked, only differently.

nodes.label: AES-SIV-CMAC Name Transform With Parent-Chain AAD
nodes.norm_label: aes-siv-cmac name transform with parent-chain aad
nodes.rationale: D4-D7, D11: each segment is encrypted with AES-SIV-CMAC (RFC 5297) under a 512-bit name key, binding the version label s3ep-name-v1, the segment depth and the ciphertext of its parent chain — so a subtree the backend moves or duplicates fails to decrypt in its new place, while each segment stays verifiable without decrypting its ancestors, which is what a listing needs. The bucket is deliberately excluded, mirroring the storage format, so a ciphertext bucket can be replicated wholesale. Encoded base64url unpadded (no '/', no URL escaping, case-sensitive). The name key is one random 64-byte key per deployment, wrapped by the active KEK and never derived from it — deriving it would rename every object on every KEK rotation, and a KMS-backed provider has no raw key to derive from. Names that do not decrypt are dropped and counted rather than failing the whole listing, which would be a one-object denial of service.

nodes.label: The Name Transform Lives at the Backend Boundary
nodes.norm_label: the name transform lives at the backend boundary
nodes.rationale: D8, D14, D15, D17: applied at exactly one place, in both directions, so above it every key is the client's — signatures, associated data, logs and error documents correct by construction — and no request handler ever sees a stored key. Because the segment chain binds the client's key into the associated data, the stored bytes are byte-identical whether the feature is on or off: enabling it on a populated bucket is a rename pass, and rotating the name key renames the bucket rather than re-encrypting it. Transforming at each backend call site was rejected: forgetting one is silent. A stored key appears only at debug level and never in the same log entry as its plaintext, because many deployments ship logs to the provider that holds the bucket, and such a line is the mapping table this design refuses to store.

nodes.label: Performance Is Measured Before and After, Never Asserted
nodes.norm_label: performance is measured before and after, never asserted
nodes.rationale: D1-D5: a performance change carries a benchmark before and after — fresh stack, at least three runs, median, baseline on the same machine at the pre-change commit; where two paths exist both are measured and the loser is deleted, never left configurable or reachable by accident of middleware composition; the decision rule and the instrument's bias are written down before the run; a regression stops the work. Twice a confident claim was wrong about its own tree: a pooled response buffer blamed on a monitoring flag that turned out not to matter (the real finding was a capability loss on every route), and a '42% crypto floor' of which ten points sat under the proxy-to-backend TLS records.

nodes.label: SSE-C Refused With 501 Until Every Verb Carries the Key
nodes.norm_label: sse-c refused with 501 until every verb carries the key
nodes.rationale: D6: the three x-amz-server-side-encryption-customer-* headers are refused with 501 NotImplemented naming the header. The asymmetry earns the refusal — no read path carries the key back, so accepting it on upload alone writes objects the proxy could never read: a silent time bomb rather than a silent drop. Forwarding on PUT only was rejected as strictly worse; either every verb carries the key or none does.

nodes.label: Uniform Storage-Header Forwarding on Every Upload Path
nodes.norm_label: uniform storage-header forwarding on every upload path
nodes.rationale: D3/D12: single PUT, internal multipart and CreateMultipartUpload forward the same set (server-side encryption and its KMS key id, tagging, storage class, acl and grants, object-lock mode/retain-until/legal-hold, website-redirect-location) through one shared decision. Documented with consequences: tags and user metadata are a plaintext index at the backend, a public ACL makes a public ciphertext object, object lock defends against a compromised credential not a compromised backend, and a forwarded server-side-encryption header is the backend encrypting its own copy.

nodes.label: A Client Metadata Key Inside the Namespace Is Refused
nodes.norm_label: a client metadata key inside the namespace is refused
nodes.rationale: D6: PUT and CreateMultipartUpload answer 400 InvalidArgument naming the offending key, identically on all three write paths; the key is not stripped, renamed or stored. Case-sensitive comparison on the single-part paths let a key differing only in case survive and collide at the backend, leaving four of ten uploads permanently undecryptable — a denial-of-restore any client can trigger. Silently stripping was rejected: because the response filter is a prefix test, the client would lose the key twice and be told 200 both times.

nodes.label: Listing Parameters Honoured or Refused, max-keys Validated
nodes.norm_label: listing parameters honoured or refused, max-keys validated
nodes.rationale: D7/D8/D10: prefix, delimiter, max-keys, continuation-token, start-after, fetch-owner, encoding-type on ListObjectsV2 and their ListObjects/ListBuckets counterparts are honoured or refused, never dropped, and pagination fields are emitted so a client can page to exhaustion. max-keys: absent leaves the backend default, 0-1000 forwarded verbatim, above 1000 clamped (because S3 clamps), negative or non-integer answers 400 InvalidArgument. HEAD /{bucket} becomes a real existence check rather than a listing with page size zero, which changes which backend permission it needs.

nodes.label: Every Declared Client Checksum Is Verified Against the Plaintext
nodes.norm_label: every declared client checksum is verified against the plaintext
nodes.rationale: D1-D3, amended 2026-09-09: verified against the received plaintext with aws-chunked framing stripped, before encryption, on every write path; crc32, crc32c, crc64nvme, sha1, sha256 and Content-MD5, as header or trailer. The proposed encryption.verify_upload_digests key was withdrawn before it was built — the client chooses the algorithm and with it the cost, and dropping a declared digest behind a 200 is exactly what ADR 0007 forbids. Costs were measured 2026-09-09: MD5 about 10x the AES-GCM pass per byte, SHA-1/SHA-256 about 2.5x where hardware accelerates them, published as a table rather than gated. The client-to-proxy leg is the last place plaintext exists and nothing else defends it.

nodes.label: Multi-Object Delete Must Carry a Verified Body Digest
nodes.norm_label: multi-object delete must carry a verified body digest
nodes.rationale: D14, added 2026-09-09: a request with neither Content-MD5 nor x-amz-checksum-* is refused with 400 InvalidRequest, and the digest is verified against the raw body before the document is parsed. The body is a few kilobytes and the operation is destructive, so there is no cost argument and every reason for the check. Related rules: a trailer named in X-Amz-Trailer that never arrives is a failed verification (D5), mismatch is 400 BadDigest and malformed is 400 InvalidDigest (D6), and the verdict lands before anything is committed (D7).

nodes.label: SigV4 in Both Forms Against Static Configured Clients
nodes.norm_label: sigv4 in both forms against static configured clients
nodes.rationale: D1-D3, D10: the Authorization-header form and the pre-signed query form are both first-class on every authenticated route, against static s3_clients entries (access key id >= 8 chars, secret >= 16, duplicates a startup error). Every request is checked for a bounded Authorization header, a well-shaped credential scope with service s3 and terminator aws4_request, a known access key, a timestamp inside the skew window both ways, a matching credential date, and the full signature compared in constant time; failures answer a fixed message per S3 error code and never echo the attempted key id. Supporting only one form is not an option — a backup tool signs uploads and hands out pre-signed URLs for its own downloads.

nodes.label: The Integration Suite Runs Over Both Plain HTTP and TLS
nodes.norm_label: the integration suite runs over both plain http and tls
nodes.rationale: D5: both runs must be green, because the AWS SDK emits STREAMING-UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD-TRAILER framing only over HTTPS. Measured on the branch that closed it: a full TLS run hits the buffered chunked path 718 times, a plain-HTTP run zero times, and a defect that stored chunk framing as object payload lived in exactly that gap. One transport is not a cheaper sample of the other; it is a different code path. If wall-clock cost becomes a problem the runs are split into parallel jobs, never dropped.

nodes.label: The Proxy Serves Any S3 Client
nodes.norm_label: the proxy serves any s3 client
nodes.rationale: D1-D4: compatibility is argued from S3 semantics, never from what one observed client sends; 'no client in scope does X' is not an argument unless X is impossible in S3, and a defect found through one client is fixed for every client it applies to. Forced by a storage-header brief that argued per header from one client's behaviour and produced five wrong answers out of six — only the customer-provided-key refusal survived re-checking against S3 semantics. Tiered support was rejected because 'best effort' becomes the standing answer to any defect the one supported tool does not hit.

nodes.label: Forward It or Refuse It, Never Silently Drop It
nodes.norm_label: forward it or refuse it, never silently drop it
nodes.rationale: D1/D2: a request is honoured or refused with a named S3 error and matching status; accepting, discarding part of it and answering success is forbidden for headers, bodies, sub-resources and query parameters alike. Anything that does not touch object-content confidentiality is the client's business and is forwarded, not adjudicated. Probed concretely: a PUT with server-side-encryption, storage class, tagging and ACL answered 200 with four silent drops. The sharpest instance was already closed — an unrouted bucket sub-resource executed the base operation, so DELETE /{bucket}?encryption deleted the bucket.

nodes.label: Required Pod Anti-Affinity

nodes.label: Hardened Pod and Container Security Context
nodes.norm_label: hardened pod and container security context
nodes.rationale: Non-root uid/gid 1001, RuntimeDefault seccomp, all capabilities dropped, no privilege escalation and a read-only root filesystem - the writable /tmp emptyDir exists so the read-only root filesystem stays possible.

nodes.label: Health Check Sidecar

nodes.label: Vault Dev Server with Transit Engine
nodes.norm_label: vault dev server with transit engine
nodes.rationale: Runs in dev mode with the transit secrets engine enabled and two example keys (app-key aes256-gcm96, rsa-key rsa-2048) prepared for a future KMS-backed KEK provider.

nodes.label: License JWT Volume Mount
nodes.rationale: The license secret (license.existingSecret or license.jwt) is projected to /app/license/license.jwt read-only; the ConfigMap only emits license_file when one of the two is set, so the mount path and the config key must agree or the startup license gate fails.

nodes.label: Namespace/Release Job Label Relabeling
nodes.rationale: metricRelabelings rewrite the job label to <namespace>/<release> and add helm_release, so several releases of the same chart in different namespaces stay distinguishable in one Prometheus and in the shared Grafana dashboard.

nodes.label: Multi-Tenant Grafana Job Labels
nodes.rationale: Installing the same chart into production and development namespaces yields job labels production/prod-s3-proxy and development/dev-s3-proxy, which is why one shared dashboard can serve several releases.

nodes.label: Image Supply-Chain Attestation
nodes.rationale: SBOM, provenance, reproducible builds, build attestation and OCI annotations are enabled together, plus vulnerability, secret and license scanning - the image is meant to be verifiable, not just scanned once.

nodes.label: Evaluation-Tuned Chart Defaults
nodes.rationale: The chart defaults (single replica, no PodDisruptionBudget, no NetworkPolicy, no autoscaling, no TLS) are deliberately chosen for trying the proxy out, not for production. Production deployments are expected to start from values-production.yaml instead of hardening the defaults piecemeal.

nodes.label: PodDisruptionBudget minAvailable/maxUnavailable Exclusivity
nodes.rationale: Exactly one of minAvailable or maxUnavailable must be set; the chart fails the render if both or neither are given. maxUnavailable is the documented default because it stays drainable at any replica count, while minAvailable equal to the replica count blocks node drains indefinitely.

nodes.label: Chart Secrets Management Policy
nodes.rationale: Secrets are never stored in values files; they are passed via --set at install time or sourced from an external secret manager, so a checked-in or published values file never carries credentials.

nodes.label: PDB Render-Time Fail Guard
nodes.rationale: The template calls Helm fail when both minAvailable and maxUnavailable are set, and again when neither is; the misconfiguration is turned into a render error instead of a PDB the API server would reject or a silently empty spec.

nodes.label: No Default AES Key Rule
nodes.rationale: The default provider config sets aes_key to the environment reference ${S3EP_AES_KEY} rather than a literal key: a literal key shipped in a published chart is a key everyone has, so any release taking the default would encrypt every object under a publicly known KEK.

nodes.label: PDB Disabled by Default
nodes.rationale: The PDB is off by default because the default deployment runs a single replica: a PDB would then block every voluntary eviction and node drains or cluster upgrades would hang indefinitely.

nodes.label: Single cert-manager Certificate Rule
nodes.rationale: cert-manager issues the certificate into the secret referenced by ingress.tls; the cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer ingress annotation must not additionally be set because ingress-shim would then create a second Certificate for the same secret.

nodes.label: Ingress Streaming Annotations
nodes.rationale: proxy-body-size 0 and proxy-request-buffering off keep nginx from buffering large objects, so uploads stream through the proxy end to end instead of being materialized at the ingress - this preserves the streaming memory footprint the proxy is built for.

nodes.label: GOCOVER Instrumented Build and Shutdown Grace
nodes.norm_label: gocover instrumented build and shutdown grace
nodes.rationale: GOCOVER=1 builds an instrumented proxy writing to /coverage. Coverage counters are only flushed on a clean exit and the proxy waits up to its 30s shutdown timeout for in-flight requests, so stop_grace_period is raised to 45s - the 10s docker default would SIGKILL the process and throw the coverage data away.

nodes.label: Why a Second TLS Proxy Instance Exists
nodes.norm_label: why a second tls proxy instance exists
nodes.rationale: aws-sdk-go-v2 only emits STREAMING-UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD-TRAILER framing and checksum trailers over HTTPS, so the plain-HTTP endpoint structurally cannot exercise the default behaviour of a modern SDK client. Both endpoints stay: HTTP covers the non-trailer code path, TLS the trailer decoder.

nodes.label: Provider Selection by s3ep-kek-fingerprint
nodes.rationale: D4/D5: the object records s3ep-kek-fingerprint and s3ep-kek-algorithm; on read the proxy selects the provider whose fingerprint matches, with no default provider and no trial decryption. The fingerprint is derived by the provider from its own key material so it cannot drift, is public, and links deployments that share a key. Trial decryption was rejected because against an unauthenticated wrap it cannot distinguish success from failure.

nodes.label: Authenticated AES-256-GCM Key Wrap with Per-Wrap Salt
nodes.norm_label: authenticated aes-256-gcm key wrap with per-wrap salt
nodes.rationale: D6-D9: fingerprint and wrapping key are both HKDF-SHA256 expansions of the master key under distinct labels (s3ep-kek-fingerprint, s3ep-kek-wrap-v1 concatenated with a fresh 16-byte salt), never the key itself. s3ep-encrypted-dek becomes salt || nonce || ciphertext || tag, 76 bytes, with associated data s3ep-dek-wrap-v1; a tampered wrapped key fails with its own error before any object byte is read. The per-wrap salt removes the 2^32 message bound that would need a wrap counter nothing in the product counts. AES-KWP (RFC 5649) was attractive at 40 bytes and no message bound but lost on dependencies: not in the standard library, and a wrap format must not depend on a library decision taken after it.

nodes.label: Key Admission Rules (No Passphrases)
nodes.rationale: D3-D5: aes_key must be standard base64 of exactly 32 bytes with no verbatim fallback, and startup refuses a key whose 32 decoded bytes are all printable ASCII or contain fewer than 16 distinct byte values. Entropy at the source is the only lever against a guessable key, since the adversary holds the wrapped data key and a tag forever and works offline. Pricing passphrases with Argon2id was rejected: 40-60 bits of entropy survives no work factor. The rules are an accidental-passphrase heuristic, not an entropy proof.

nodes.label: The KMS Fingerprint Identifies the Key, Not Its Material
nodes.norm_label: the kms fingerprint identifies the key, not its material
nodes.rationale: D8, plus the 2026-09-07 amendment: the proxy never holds the key so the fingerprint is derived from the key's identity (its KMS address) and the key version must not take part in it — a proxy restarted after a routine in-KMS rotation would otherwise publish a different fingerprint for the same logical key and could no longer select the provider for objects it wrote. This is the one fingerprint in the design that is not a function of key material.

nodes.label: No Working Key Material or License Token in the Repository
nodes.norm_label: no working key material or license token in the repository
nodes.rationale: D1-D4, D8: no key encryption key, private key, license token or test CA key in any example configuration, chart values, deployment values, fixture or document — a file named 'example' is held to the same rule as one named 'production', because the example is what gets copied. Material a local stack needs is generated on demand into an ignored path and exported as ${S3EP_AES_KEY}, referenced identically everywhere, with no fallback and no default key. Where a generator produces material that must agree with itself, no half is tracked: a tracked certificate stops matching a freshly generated key and the failure points at everything except the checkout. The concrete defect was a chart shipping a working 256-bit key as its default, so an install that configured nothing encrypted under a repository-public key and succeeded.

nodes.label: Custody by Injection Is Not a KMS
nodes.norm_label: custody by injection is not a kms
nodes.rationale: D2: delivering the local key through ${S3EP_AES_KEY} from a Vault agent, operator or external-secrets controller works with no code and is supported, but the key is in process memory for the process lifetime and a compromised process yields it. The two look alike in a deployment diagram and differ completely in what a compromise yields; declaring injection to be KMS support was rejected as a documentation claim the product does not honour.

nodes.label: Pre-Signed URL Expiry Cap and Uniform Clock Skew
nodes.norm_label: pre-signed url expiry cap and uniform clock skew
nodes.rationale: D4-D6, D9: s3_security keeps exactly two enforced keys. max_clock_skew_seconds (default 900) governs both forms — it previously worked only on the pre-signed path while the header form, which carries all the traffic, compared against a compile-time 900. max_presign_expiry_seconds defaults to 3600 with a hard cap of the S3 maximum 604800, enforced at validation and at use; X-Amz-Expires is mandatory and positive so a URL cannot extend its own lifetime. Seven days of bearer capability is the wrong default for a proxy whose purpose is to bound exposure. Residual: replay inside the validity window is undefended, there is no nonce store.

nodes.label: No Wall Clock on a Transfer
nodes.norm_label: no wall clock on a transfer
nodes.rationale: D1-D3, D6: no wall-clock budget on reading a request body or writing a response body; only the header phase (30 s) and the idle keep-alive connection (60 s) are bounded, and bounding a client that occupies a connection without progress is the ingress's job. The two fixed 30-second budgets made the maximum servable object a function of client bandwidth — roughly 3.6 GB at 1 Gbit/s, 375 MB at 100 Mbit/s — resetting healthy transfers mid-stream. Configurable budgets were rejected because the only correct value is effectively infinite; raising them was rejected because rarer failures are harder to diagnose. The defect survived every benchmark because the suites run on loopback with parts in the low tens of megabytes.

nodes.label: shutdown_timeout Is the Only Server-Side Transfer Budget
nodes.norm_label: shutdown_timeout is the only server-side transfer budget
nodes.rationale: D4/D5/D8: the drain waits for in-flight transfers up to shutdown_timeout (30 s when unset or zero) and no other fixed shutdown deadline exists; the Kubernetes chart derives terminationGracePeriodSeconds as shutdown_timeout + 5 so the platform does not kill the process before the budget expires. No new key is introduced for any of these budgets. Cost: pod termination waits for the slowest in-flight transfer, so one long transfer delays a rolling restart by the full budget.

nodes.label: A Configuration Key Exists Only If Code Reads It
nodes.norm_label: a configuration key exists only if code reads it
nodes.rationale: D1/D2/D9/D10: a new key lands with the code that reads it and a test that proves the effect; a key with no reader is deleted, never documented as aspirational. Deleted: six s3_security keys (rate limiting, request and failed-attempt thresholds, unblock timer, strict signature validation, security logging) with the per-address failure map behind them, s3_backend.use_tls, optimizations.clean_http_transfer_chunked, the legacy top-level backend block and its migration, and (2026-09-09) optimizations.streaming_buffer_size and enable_adaptive_buffering. Removing a key is a breaking change announced only in release notes, because the loader ignores unknown keys silently. The rule is a discipline enforced by review, not a mechanism.

nodes.label: No Rate Limiting and No Per-Address Blocking
nodes.norm_label: no rate limiting and no per-address blocking
nodes.rationale: D7/D8: the proxy performs no rate limiting and no per-address blocking and ships no key suggesting otherwise; the client address is a log field, never an identity, so there is no trusted-proxy list to configure. Per-address limiting is the wrong instrument — one legitimate S3 client is one authenticated identity bursting thousands of requests from one address, and clients behind NAT or an ingress share one — and a 16-character secret is not guessable, so brute-force protection at this door is a fiction. The failure map it replaces was keyed on caller-chosen X-Forwarded-For, never evicted, compared against a hardcoded threshold, and written unsynchronised: two parallel unauthenticated requests were a remote kill switch, since a concurrent map write terminates the Go runtime and is not a recoverable panic.

nodes.label: No Compatibility Is Owed for Data at Rest
nodes.norm_label: no compatibility is owed for data at rest
nodes.rationale: D1/D2/D10: a major release may change the stored layout, the metadata keys and the key-identifier derivation with no migration path and no read path for what came before, on the stated precondition — confirmed with the owner per breaking release — that no deployment is known to hold data that must survive. Everything that forces operator action ships in one major so one upgrade costs one migration. The choice was never break-or-not but break-or-ship-two-readers, and the second reader is the whole decrypt path the new format deletes, kept alive next to its replacement and scheduled for deletion anyway. Lazy re-encryption on read was rejected: it turns a read into a write the client never asked for and never terminates.

nodes.norm_label: testing strategy: unit, integration, velero e2e
nodes.rationale: Integration and Velero e2e tests may never be disabled, skipped or removed: they are the end-user experience. Integration needs ./start-demo.sh; the Velero suite needs a kind cluster from e2e-up.sh, the same script CI runs so a workstation and a runner cannot drift apart, and a license token or the proxy pod never becomes ready.

nodes.label: License expiry stops the proxy
nodes.rationale: The validator checks hourly and exits once the license expires, and without a valid license only type: none is permitted, so an expired license means no decryption path at all and every object in the bucket is unreadable until the proxy is relicensed (ADR 0016).

nodes.label: Reporting a vulnerability
nodes.rationale: A private GitHub security advisory is the only private route, and it has not been exercised. The repository carries no SECURITY.md and no dedicated security contact; CONTRIBUTING.md points only at public issues and discussions.

nodes.label: An ADR Carries No References Into the Code
nodes.norm_label: an adr carries no references into the code
nodes.rationale: D7/D8: no file paths, line numbers, function, type or package names, no links into the tree, so a reader acts on the decision without opening the repository and the ADR does not go stale when a file is renamed. The product's own vocabulary is not a code reference and is named exactly: configuration keys, s3ep-* metadata keys, S3 error codes, header and algorithm names, release versions and shipped commands. A comment or commit that must point at pending work points at the ADR by number and title.

nodes.label: ADR Index and Ground Rules
nodes.rationale: Groups the 23 ADRs into Foundations, Stored format, The S3 surface, Operation and Process, and fixes the file format: NNNN-kebab-case-title.md with Status, Context, Decision (D1..Dn in present tense), Consequences, Alternatives Considered, Residual risks, References. Ground rules: English only, a decision not an implementation, no code references, say what is decided separately from what is built, and mark what was not verified.

nodes.label: Documentation States What the Code Verifies (D10)
nodes.norm_label: documentation states what the code verifies (d10)
nodes.rationale: While a rule is decided but not built, the README and security architecture say the backend must be treated as trusted infrastructure and name the unverified reads. The claim is upgraded in the release that earns it. Accepted cost: the product publishes in its own README that its integrity modes do not refuse a tampered object on one path.

nodes.label: The ADR Is Written in the Session the Decision Is Taken
nodes.norm_label: the adr is written in the session the decision is taken
nodes.rationale: D1/D2/D9/D11: one file per decision family, written when the decision is taken rather than when the implementation lands, amended in place when it changes (Decision states the new rule, Status records the amendment and date, the superseded rule is marked rather than deleted), with Status saying plainly what is built and Decision in the present tense either way. Writing the ADR when the work lands was what was being done: it leaves long-running decisions unwritten for a whole release, by which time the rejected options have been forgotten. Accepted cost: ADRs describe behaviour that does not exist yet, so a reader who skips Status is misled by an accurate document.

nodes.label: Finish, Document, Delete: The Ticket Lifecycle
nodes.norm_label: finish, document, delete: the ticket lifecycle
nodes.rationale: D3-D6, D10: a ticket is a work list and nothing else, closed by deleting the file after the decision moves into an ADR and the user-facing consequence into the README or security architecture; nothing outside the ticket directory references a ticket, and work-tracking labels die with it. The backlog had grown to roughly twelve thousand lines mixing outstanding work, decisions, verification notes and closed history, with one index page defining over a hundred labels in five parallel series. Twenty-nine source files carried ticket numbers, so a finished ticket could never be deleted; identifiers drifted while citations did not. Archiving closed tickets was rejected: an archive is a place where everything is kept and nothing is read.

nodes.label: Authenticated Trailer (Length and Sealed CRC32C)
nodes.rationale: D6/D13, amended 2026-09-09: a 40-byte trailer seals the total plaintext length together with a CRC32C of the whole plaintext, checked before the last segment is released, so truncation or extension at any segment boundary is detected. The checksum moved out of the metadata set because metadata is sent before the first body byte on every write path and the checksum exists only after the last. It is sealed, never in the clear, because a cleartext checksum of a small object is a guessing oracle for the backend. SHA-256 was rejected: 2.5x the AES-GCM pass and not combinable across out-of-order or re-uploaded parts.

nodes.label: Tail-First Whole-Object Read with If-Match
nodes.rationale: D14: HEAD is answered from one ranged read of the last 40 bytes; a whole-object GET reads the last 65604 bytes first and, when that does not cover the object, fetches the remainder under If-Match on the first response's entity tag so a replacement answers 412 before any body byte. Every stored byte is fetched exactly once. Two parallel requests were rejected because every small-object read would then cost two requests, which is where request count hurts most.

nodes.label: Bounded Short-Part Buffer for the Trailer
nodes.norm_label: bounded short-part buffer for the trailer
nodes.rationale: D4/D5, amended 2026-09-09: the trailer rides an extra part when the client's last part is >= 5 MiB (leaving 9999 usable part numbers), otherwise the short part is held as ciphertext and re-uploaded with the trailer at Complete. Two bounds: at most one short part per session (a second answers EntityTooSmall at upload time, where the client can still act), and a global cap optimizations.multipart_short_part_buffer_size, default 64 MiB, minimum 5 MiB, over which a short part answers SlowDown 503. It is a configuration key because it is memory the operator budgets against the container limit — a cap the operator cannot lower reaches the OOM kill before it reaches SlowDown. S3's 5 MiB non-final part minimum was verified directly against MinIO RELEASE.2025-09-07T16-13-09Z.

nodes.label: The Proxy Serves Its Own Sealed CRC32C on Whole-Object Reads
nodes.norm_label: the proxy serves its own sealed crc32c on whole-object reads
nodes.rationale: D10/D10a: never the backend's checksum (that describes ciphertext), but the value recorded at upload and sealed in the trailer, served as x-amz-checksum-crc32c on a whole-object GET and on HEAD, with no configuration key; a ranged read carries none because the value covers the whole object. It is never recomputed from what is about to be sent — a checksum over the same buffer that may be corrupt proves nothing — which makes it the only control that can catch a fault in the proxy's own assembly of already-verified plaintext.

nodes.label: Memory Is Held by a Test on a Hard Bound
nodes.norm_label: memory is held by a test on a hard bound
nodes.rationale: D14/D15: the test samples process_resident_memory_bytes from the proxy's own metrics endpoint and asserts peak-minus-idle against a bound expressed in streaming_segment_size, multipart_upload_concurrency and (2026-09-09) multipart_short_part_buffer_size; logging the number instead of failing on it is not sufficient. GOMEMLIMIT is set explicitly as a visible value defaulting to 80% of the container limit, GOGC keeps its default and is never disabled while any client-controlled full-body allocation exists, and the value ships only if the memory test stays green and the benchmark shows a gain.

nodes.label: Fail Closed on Foreign Objects (InvalidObjectState 403)
nodes.rationale: D5: under an encrypting provider an object with no proxy metadata, or in a format this proxy does not write, is refused on GET, HEAD and ranged GET with InvalidObjectState and HTTP 403, with no opt-out. Passing it through with a warning was rejected as 'the substitution attack, with a warning attached'. Amended 2026-09-09: such a bucket is not migrated, its content is uploaded through the proxy from the source.

nodes.label: Well-Formedness Guard on the Stored-to-Plaintext Size Function
nodes.norm_label: well-formedness guard on the stored-to-plaintext size function
nodes.rationale: D12/D12a: plaintext length is a pure function of the stored length, so it is reported without a per-object round trip. Because the adversary reports the stored length freely and the formulas answer for lengths no writer can produce, the function carries a reachability guard (P >= 0 and n == 0 && P == 0 or (n-1)*S < P <= n*S). Verified exhaustively over P = 0..5S+5 plus 12 MiB and 1 GiB. Not a security control — the trailer authenticates the length — but a rejected length is a 500 rather than a fabricated size in a HEAD.

nodes.label: Every Reported Size Describes the Plaintext
nodes.norm_label: every reported size describes the plaintext
nodes.rationale: D1-D3: GET, HEAD and every listing entry report the plaintext size, computed by arithmetic over the storage format from the stored size alone. The concrete failure is bandwidth: aws s3 sync, rclone and every synchronising client compare listing sizes and re-transfer everything, forever, silently. Under the none provider and for stored sizes no plaintext maps to, the stored size is reported verbatim rather than a number being invented.

nodes.label: There Is No Migration; the Data Is Uploaded Again From Its Source
nodes.norm_label: there is no migration; the data is uploaded again from its source
nodes.rationale: D3-D6, amended 2026-09-09: no re-encryption job, no in-place converter, no dual-format reader, no procedure for extracting plaintext from a bucket the new release cannot read. An object the new release refuses is deleted or left to expire. 'Detect the format and read whatever fits' was rejected outright — the format would be decided by metadata the backend can edit, so the backend picks the reader. The release notes state which lines stop being readable, which keys change, which values now refuse startup, and that one proxy version runs at a time; the upgrade is rehearsed once on a running stack, with an old object answering InvalidObjectState 403 and a fresh upload matching by SHA-256.

nodes.label: All Three Write Paths Produce the Identical Byte Layout
nodes.norm_label: all three write paths produce the identical byte layout
nodes.rationale: D11: single PUT, proxy-driven multipart and client-driven multipart write the same layout, with the data key, wrapped key and complete metadata set existing before the first backend byte, so no object is rewritten after completion to attach late metadata. This deletes the post-completion self-copy and with it the hard failure above 5 GiB, and makes segments independent so parts no longer have to be encrypted in sequence.

nodes.label: No Post-Completion Rewrite (Removing the 5 GiB Ceiling)
nodes.norm_label: no post-completion rewrite (removing the 5 gib ceiling)
nodes.rationale: D8: every metadata value is known before the first backend byte and set at CreateMultipartUpload, so the finished object is never rewritten. The self-copy it replaces was a full server-side rewrite of every multipart object, doubling versions on a versioned bucket and hard-capped at 5 GiB, so every larger multipart upload failed after all bytes were transferred and the upload committed — leaving an object the proxy cannot read back. Attaching the late-bound value by object tagging was rejected: a proxy-owned tag namespace, an extra read-side request, and a crash window in which the stored object carries no encryption metadata.

nodes.label: A Query String Containing ';' Is Refused (Parser/Router Disagreement)
nodes.norm_label: a query string containing ';' is refused (parser/router disagreement)
nodes.rationale: D13, added 2026-09-09: refused with 400 InvalidArgument after authentication and before routing. The standard library's query parser drops every &-separated segment containing a ';' while the router splits on both characters, so a PUT with a ';' fell through to the plain object PUT with an empty parsed query and overwrote the object — authenticating cleanly, because the canonical query string was built from the same parsed query. Refusing the character closes the whole class of parser disagreement, not one instance.

nodes.label: The x-amz-* Namespace Is the Query Allowlist
nodes.norm_label: the x-amz-* namespace is the query allowlist
nodes.rationale: D9: an unrouted query parameter is refused by name and never executes the base operation for its method; x-amz-* parameters are protocol and admitted everywhere. A literal list of SDK parameter names was tried and broke — the SDK added a checksum-mode parameter to every pre-signed GetObject URL, so every pre-signed download was refused. No S3 sub-resource lives in that namespace and every query parameter is covered by the signature.

nodes.label: One Bring-Up Script for Workstation and CI
nodes.norm_label: one bring-up script for workstation and ci
nodes.rationale: D7/D8/D10: the e2e environment is created and destroyed by the same scripts everywhere, so a workstation and a runner cannot drift into 'green in CI, red on my machine'; re-testing reloads a freshly built image rather than recreating the cluster. Pinned upstream versions move as one manually reviewed group, against a repository default of automatic merges, because a backup client and the chart that installs it are versioned separately. The environment must run the configuration the documentation recommends, not the client's insecure defaults — a suite exercising a configuration nobody is told to run is evidence about the wrong system.

nodes.label: Listener failure asymmetry (fatal proxy, non-fatal monitoring)

nodes.label: Startup sequence: config, license, metrics, then listeners
nodes.description: The linear startup ordering visible as runProxy's callee fan-out.
nodes.norm_label: startup sequence: config, license, metrics, then listeners
nodes.rationale: The graph shows a strict ordering inside one function rather than a layered init chain: cobra.OnInitialize runs config.InitConfig, then runProxy calls config.LoadAndStartLicense, validates the license, publishes SetServerInfo/SetLicenseInfo, and only afterwards constructs monitoring.NewServer and proxy.NewServer. Keeping the whole sequence in one function is what makes the ordering auditable - no package-level init side effects decide whether the proxy comes up.

nodes.label: Graceful shutdown drain with atomic request counter
nodes.description: Ticker-plus-deadline drain loop reading the in-flight counter maintained by the injected request tracker.
nodes.norm_label: graceful shutdown drain with atomic request counter
nodes.rationale: Shutdown state lives in main, not in the proxy package: runProxy flips it with sync/atomic.StoreInt32 and hands the server two closures (SetShutdownStateHandler, SetRequestTracker) instead of importing shutdown logic into the server. runProxy$6 then polls sync/atomic.LoadInt64 on a ticker against a single time.After deadline. The inversion keeps the proxy package free of process lifecycle concerns and gives one place where the drain deadline is enforced - important here because an in-flight multipart or streaming encryption must not be cut mid-object.

nodes.label: License startup gate
nodes.description: Validation of the license JWT before any listener is constructed.
nodes.rationale: The token is read in main itself (os.Getenv for S3EP_LICENSE_TOKEN, os.ReadFile for the license file, strings.TrimSpace on the result) and validated by license.ValidateLicense before proxy.NewServer appears in the call order. The gate therefore sits in the process entrypoint, not in the request path: an unlicensed process never binds the S3 listener, so no request can ever be served under an invalid license.
