nodes.rationale: Only ${VAR} is expanded, never bare $VAR, so passwords containing $ are safe; an unset or empty reference makes the proxy refuse to start rather than silently fall back. The shipped example configs carry demo keys inline with the ${VAR} lines commented out, so passing the variables changes nothing until the config is edited.

nodes.label: Provider comparison: RSA, AES, None
nodes.rationale: RSA is recommended for production (self-contained, no KMS, manual key management); AES is simplest and fastest but one master key wraps every DEK, so a compromise affects all data; None is testing only and stores plaintext at rest.

nodes.label: H-8 The AES KEK fingerprint is a plain hash of the key
nodes.norm_label: h-8 the aes kek fingerprint is a plain hash of the key
nodes.rationale: hex(SHA-256(KEK)) is written to every object in the clear. Harmless for a 256-bit generated key, but it turns a low-entropy or published key into an offline verification oracle for a dictionary attack, and it links deployments: two buckets with the same fingerprint provably share a KEK. ADR 0004 replaces it with an HKDF expansion under its own label, at the cost of an object-format change.

nodes.label: KEK providers: aes, rsa, none, tink
nodes.norm_label: kek providers: aes, rsa, none, tink
nodes.rationale: aes wraps the DEK with AES-CTR and no authentication tag, so a flipped bit in the wrapped DEK yields a different DEK without error (the authenticated wrap is ADR 0004); rsa uses RSA-OAEP-SHA256 and requires both keys, so encrypt-only deployments are impossible today; none writes no metadata and stores plaintext; tink is refused by config validation and is not a production option however CLAUDE.md presents it.

nodes.label: KEK rotation by fingerprint
nodes.rationale: Add the new provider, point the alias at it, restart: writes use the new KEK and reads select the provider matching s3ep-kek-fingerprint. Fingerprints are derived, not configured, so they cannot drift; removing an old provider makes its objects permanently unreadable, because there is no re-encryption job. The RSA fingerprint keeps only the low byte of the exponent, a known defect that cannot be corrected without changing every RSA fingerprint ever written.

nodes.label: Key hierarchy: KEK, DEK, object bytes, HMAC key
nodes.norm_label: key hierarchy: kek, dek, object bytes, hmac key
nodes.rationale: A 256-bit DEK from crypto/rand per object, wrapped by the KEK and stored wrapped in metadata; the HMAC key is HKDF-SHA256 from that same DEK with fixed salt and info, so it is a deterministic function of the DEK alone. Nothing else is mixed in, which is why the HMAC binds an object to its DEK and not to its name.

nodes.label: The six s3ep-* metadata keys
nodes.rationale: The prefix is validated against ^[a-z0-9-]+$ at startup because an empty prefix made every GET decide the object was unencrypted and serve ciphertext behind a 200, and a prefix with a capital never matched back (S3 lower-cases metadata keys in transit while the comparisons did not). The namespace is no longer client-writable: net/http canonicalisation let x-amz-meta-s3ep-* through a case-sensitive filter and the client value won often enough to leave objects permanently undecryptable. It is still dropped silently rather than refused with InvalidArgument, which is what ADR 0009 specifies.

nodes.label: A published chart default that was a working key
nodes.norm_label: a published chart default that was a working key
nodes.rationale: values.yaml shipped a literal aes_key and values-monitoring.yaml a real base64 AES-256 key, so any helm install that did not override it encrypted every object with a key published in this repository. Both are now ${S3EP_AES_KEY}; affected deployments must treat that data as compromised and re-write it under a new KEK.

nodes.rationale: Both public_key_pem and private_key_pem are required by the config validator, so the encrypt-only deployment the asymmetric design would allow is not configurable.

nodes.label: Complete configuration reference
nodes.rationale: Every value is marked as a built-in default or an example, and keys that reach no code path are labelled as such rather than presented as controls.

nodes.label: Start with the knowledge graph (graphify)
nodes.rationale: The committed graph under graphify-out/ is the fastest map of the subsystems, but a graph hit is a pointer, not a fact: wiki articles inherit the staleness of the documents they were built from, so everything is verified in code before it is cited. Rebuilding the graph is a manual, user-approved step, never run unprompted.

nodes.label: GET request flow
nodes.rationale: The stored dek-algorithm selects the reader: aes-ctr streams through a stateful CTR reader, aes-gcm decrypts through the envelope with the tag checked inside the cipher. An object without encrypted-dek is passed through unchanged, and cleanMetadata strips every prefixed key from the response.

nodes.label: Integrity verification modes (off, lax, strict, hybrid)
nodes.norm_label: integrity verification modes (off, lax, strict, hybrid)
nodes.rationale: strict does not abort an aes-ctr download: the verifying reader releases the plaintext before it verifies and is not constructed at all when the backend response has no Content-Length. hybrid is not a difference from strict, because both paths return the plain reader when s3ep-hmac is missing. No mode may be described as maximum security or as aborting a tampered download; the segmented-GCM format of ADR 0003 fixes this by construction.

nodes.label: orchestration.Manager facade
nodes.rationale: Business logic and state management sit in internal/orchestration and the crypto primitives in pkg/encryption, so the handlers talk to one public facade instead of to providers directly.

nodes.label: PUT request flow
nodes.rationale: Routing is decided by DecodedContentLength (a hint, not an authoritative plaintext size), the force-aes-ctr content type and the integrity mode: unknown length or HMAC-on at 5 MiB and above goes to auto-multipart, at or above streaming_threshold to the streaming reader, otherwise direct. Encryption happens exactly once, in the handler's call into the Manager.

nodes.label: Objects without s3ep-* metadata are served as-is
nodes.norm_label: objects without s3ep-* metadata are served as-is
nodes.rationale: GET and ranged GET return the stored bytes unchanged even when the active provider encrypts, so anyone who can write to the bucket can substitute an object by stripping its metadata. Never point an encrypting provider at a bucket that also holds objects the proxy did not write.

nodes.label: Ranged reads of encrypted objects
nodes.rationale: aes-ctr positions the keystream and fetches exactly the requested ciphertext window (one request, no amplification); aes-gcm must decrypt the whole object because the tag covers all of it, bounded by streaming_threshold. Content-Range always describes plaintext offsets, so the client never learns the object is stored encrypted. kopia, and therefore Velero volume restores, read almost exclusively this way.

nodes.label: Velero kopia repository password warning
nodes.rationale: Velero creates velero-repo-credentials with the hardcoded password static-passw0rd when the secret is absent, and the repository salt sits in the same bucket, so kopia's AES-GCM and content HMACs are forgeable by anyone who can read the bucket. Velero's own objects (resource tarballs with Secrets, logs, results) are never encrypted by Velero at all, so the proxy is the only protection. The secret must exist before the first backup; an existing repository keeps the password it was created with.

nodes.label: Versioned buckets and the extra self-copy version
nodes.norm_label: versioned buckets and the extra self-copy version
nodes.rationale: An encrypted multipart or auto-multipart upload writes a second version, because the encryption metadata is attached by the self-copy after completion; that later version, whose id is returned, is the one carrying the metadata.

nodes.label: ADR 0003: objects are an authenticated segment chain
nodes.norm_label: adr 0003: objects are an authenticated segment chain
nodes.rationale: Storage format v2: per-segment AEAD so a range is verifiable against the segments it overlaps, integrity inseparable from decryption, and missing metadata fails closed. It is the single fix that closes H-1, H-5 and H-6, which is why all three are documented rather than patched.

nodes.label: What aes-gcm and aes-ctr actually guarantee
nodes.norm_label: what aes-gcm and aes-ctr actually guarantee
nodes.rationale: GCM authenticates the ciphertext and binds it to the object key through AEAD associated data, so bytes cannot be moved to another key and a failure is caught before any plaintext is returned. CTR authenticates nothing in the cipher, uses no associated data, and relies on a plaintext HMAC that is checked too late; the construction is encrypt-and-MAC over the plaintext, so forgery still needs the DEK but nothing acts on a detected mismatch.

nodes.label: H-1 Ranged aes-ctr reads are not verified by the proxy
nodes.norm_label: h-1 ranged aes-ctr reads are not verified by the proxy
nodes.rationale: The whole-object HMAC cannot be checked against a partial read, so a ranged GET is authenticated by the backend and TLS only. Refusing partial reads would break every client that uses them (Velero restores become impossible) and reading a whole 20 MiB blob to verify a 32-byte read is pathological, so the answer is the per-segment AEAD of storage format v2. H-1 is a check that cannot run; H-5 is a check that runs too late.

nodes.label: H-3 Rollback and object substitution are not prevented
nodes.norm_label: h-3 rollback and object substitution are not prevented
nodes.rationale: Structural: an older version of a key is internally consistent because the proxy wrote it, and no AEAD or HMAC detects that. GCM's key binding stops bytes moving to a different key; CTR has no such binding. The only defence today is the client's own consistency checks, so backend versioning and object lock are the operator's lever.

nodes.label: H-4 Velero kopia repositories default to a published password
nodes.norm_label: h-4 velero kopia repositories default to a published password
nodes.rationale: Upstream behaviour, not a proxy defect, but it leaves the proxy as the only protection for Velero data, which is what makes H-1 uncomfortable. Setting a strong password before the first backup turns kopia into a genuine second layer and is the interim mitigation for H-1.

nodes.label: H-5 integrity_verification does not refuse a tampered aes-ctr object
nodes.norm_label: h-5 integrity_verification does not refuse a tampered aes-ctr object
nodes.rationale: Two independent routes, both pinned by tests: the verifying reader releases the plaintext before it verifies (its near-EOF branch returns the tail, and a bufio.Reader signals EOF in a separate zero-byte read), and the reader is not constructed at all when the backend answers without Content-Length, a header the adversary chooses. A third gap: an object with no s3ep-hmac is read unverified in every mode, so the 'strips one metadata key' downgrade is not hybrid-specific. A correct gated reader exists but its only entry point has no production caller, and the handler's early check returns false unconditionally. There is currently no configuration in which a tampered aes-ctr object is refused.

nodes.label: H-6 An object without encryption metadata is served as plaintext
nodes.norm_label: h-6 an object without encryption metadata is served as plaintext
nodes.rationale: Missing s3ep-* metadata is read as a none-provider pass-through even when the active provider encrypts, on both the whole-object and the ranged path. A hostile backend strips the metadata and the substitute is delivered without an error. The decided fix fails closed with a distinct error code and no opt-out knob; a bucket holding pre-existing plaintext is re-uploaded through the proxy, never read in place.

nodes.label: Decisions live in ADRs; tickets are deleted
nodes.norm_label: decisions live in adrs; tickets are deleted
nodes.rationale: An ADR states what the product does and why and carries no code references, so it stays true when the tree moves. A ticket is a work list that is closed by deleting the file; nothing outside docs/tickets/ may reference one, because a backlog that outlives its work costs focus.

nodes.label: Auto-multipart and the metadata self-copy
nodes.rationale: The encryption metadata, the HMAC above all, only exists after the last part is encrypted, and S3 CompleteMultipartUpload accepts no metadata, so the object is copied onto itself with MetadataDirective=REPLACE to attach it. Skipped for the none provider, which has nothing to attach.

nodes.label: Integrity verification: detection, not refusal
nodes.rationale: A tampered aes-gcm object is refused by its own tag before a byte is served; a tampered aes-ctr object is delivered in full behind 200 OK and the mismatch is only a log line, in every mode including strict. strict is still worth setting: it writes the HMAC the replacement format will verify against and it produces an alertable log line. Until the segment chain of ADR 0003 ships, the backend must be treated as trusted infrastructure.

nodes.label: The self-copy window
nodes.rationale: Between CompleteMultipartUpload and the metadata-attaching CopyObject the backend holds ciphertext with no encryption metadata. The copy runs on a detached 30 s context so a client disconnect cannot cancel it, and a failed copy is reported as a failed upload; but a crash in the window leaves an undecryptable object that the pass-through read path would hand to a client as if it were plaintext.
